title: Ad account bans: prevention, appeals and the same-day plan
summary: How ad accounts get restricted, how to prevent it, how to read Account Quality and appeal honestly, and exactly what to do hour by hour on the day a ban hits. You also learn to build a business that survives a restriction using only legitimate assets you own, and why evasion destroys businesses.

lessons.title: Why accounts get restricted
objectives: By the end you can name the four levels of restriction and what each one stops.
You can list the common causes of restrictions and spot them in your own setup.
You can work out your rejection rate and use it as an early warning.

steps.h: A restriction is a business event
steps.p: When an ad account stops, your spend stops, your data stops and your network sees your volume drop. For an affiliate this is a cash-flow event, not just a technical problem. This module teaches you how to prevent it, read it, appeal it and survive the day it happens.

d.b: No account, no traffic, no income
d.s: Treat account health like cash in the bank

steps.say: Let's start with a mindset shift. When an ad account stops, it's not just a technical problem. Your spend stops, your data stops, and your network sees your volume drop. For an affiliate, that's a cash-flow event. Look at the line on screen: no account, no traffic, no income. That's why we treat account health like cash in the bank. In this module you'll learn how to prevent a restriction, read it, appeal it, and survive the day it happens.

steps.h: Example: what one day offline costs
steps.p: Example numbers only. A buyer spends $300 a day at 35% ROI. That leaves about $105 profit a day. If the account is down for a week, that is about $735 of profit gone before you count team wages, lost caps or a network losing patience.
steps.more: ROI here means profit divided by spend. $300 × 0.35 = $105 profit a day. Seven days × $105 = $735. The real cost is usually higher: fixed costs such as salaries and tools keep running, a network may give your cap to another affiliate, and restarting a fresh setup often means a few days of higher cost while delivery relearns. Results vary; these figures are illustrative.
steps.say: Let's put a number on it. These are example numbers only. A buyer spends three hundred dollars a day at thirty five percent R O I, return on investment, which here means profit divided by spend. That leaves about one hundred and five dollars profit a day. If the account is down for a week, that's about seven hundred and thirty five dollars of profit gone. And that's before team wages, lost caps, or a network losing patience. Results vary, but the real cost is usually higher than it looks.

steps.p: Restrictions happen at different levels, and the level decides how much of your business stops. A rejected ad is small. A restricted personal profile or business portfolio can stop many accounts at once. Always find out which level you are dealing with first.
d: Ad rejected|one ad fails review; the account keeps running
Ad account disabled|that account cannot run ads
Business portfolio restricted|every asset inside may be affected
Personal profile restricted|that person cannot advertise or manage ads
steps.say: Restrictions happen at different levels, and the level decides how much of your business stops. Look at the four cards. A rejected ad is small: one ad fails review, and the account keeps running. A disabled ad account can't run ads at all. A restricted business portfolio can affect every asset inside it. And a restricted personal profile means that person can't advertise or manage ads. So your first question is always, which level am I dealing with?

steps.p: This is a simplified guide to the four levels. The exact effects depend on the reason and can change. Use it to judge how serious a notice is, then confirm the details in Account Quality for the specific asset.

rows: Wide if they are the only admin

steps.say: This table is a simplified guide to what each level usually stops. Read it from top to bottom. A rejected ad stops that ad, so it's narrow. An ad account stops all ads in that account, so medium. A business portfolio stops ads across its assets, so it's wide. And a personal profile stops that person's ad access, which is wide if they're the only admin. The exact effects depend on the reason and can change, so confirm the details in Account Quality for the specific asset.

steps.p: Your assets are linked. A profile admins a portfolio, the portfolio owns ad accounts, pages and pixels, and a payment method sits behind the accounts. A problem at the top can reach everything below it, which is why one weak link can stop a whole operation.
steps.say: Now look at this map, because it shows why one restriction can spread. Your profile admins a business portfolio. The portfolio owns your ad accounts, your page and your pixel or dataset. And a payment method sits behind the ad accounts, funding them. Everything is linked. So a problem at the top can reach everything below it. That's why one weak link, like a single profile or a bad payment method, can stop a whole operation.

steps.p: Most restrictions trace back to a small set of causes. The first group is about behaviour: what you advertise, how you set things up, how you pay and how you log in. Each one is something you control.
steps.more: Circumventing systems is treated very seriously. It includes things like showing reviewers a different page from users (cloaking), opening new accounts to continue after a restriction, or using other people's accounts. Platforms often restrict every linked asset when they find it. Suspicious payments include repeated declines, cards in many different names and chargebacks on charges you owed. Suspicious logins include sudden access from new countries or many people sharing one profile.
d: Policy violations|ads or pages that break advertising rules
Circumventing systems|trying to get around review or past bans
Suspicious payments|failed charges, disputes, mismatched cards
Suspicious logins|new devices, many locations, shared logins
steps.say: Most restrictions trace back to a small set of causes. This first group is about behaviour, and every one is something you control. Policy violations, meaning ads or pages that break advertising rules. Circumventing systems, like showing reviewers a different page from users, or opening new accounts after a ban. Platforms treat that very seriously. Suspicious payments, such as repeated declines, cards in many names, or chargebacks on charges you owed. And suspicious logins, like sudden access from new countries or many people sharing one profile.

steps.p: The second group is about trust and quality. A platform trusts accounts it can verify and that behave steadily. Unverified identity, sudden spend jumps, poor landing pages and regulated offers without permission all raise risk signals.
d: Unverified identity|no business or identity verification
Sudden spend spikes|$20 a day to $500 overnight
Low-quality landers|slow, misleading or mismatched pages
Restricted categories|gambling, finance or crypto without authorization
steps.say: The second group is about trust and quality. A platform trusts accounts it can verify and that behave steadily. Look at the cards. Unverified identity, with no business or identity verification. Sudden spend spikes, like going from twenty dollars a day to five hundred overnight. Low-quality landers that are slow, misleading or don't match the ad. And restricted categories, such as gambling, finance or crypto, run without authorization. Each one raises a risk signal.

steps.p: Trading, gambling, crypto and some financial products are restricted categories. Ads usually need Meta's authorization or must meet extra requirements, and they must follow local law. Rules differ by country and change, so check Meta's current policy pages and the law before you run.

d.text: Running restricted-category ads without the required authorization is a common cause of disabled accounts. Check current requirements per country before launch.

steps.p: Rejected ads are the first signal that something is wrong. Track your rejection rate every week. A rising rate means your copy, creatives or landers are drifting towards trouble long before a full restriction arrives.
d: Ads rejected
Ads submitted
Rejection rate
steps.say: Here's your early-warning number. Look at the equation: ads rejected, divided by ads submitted, equals your rejection rate. Rejected ads are the first signal that something is wrong. Track this rate every week. If it starts rising, your copy, creatives or landers are drifting toward trouble, often long before a full restriction arrives. It's a simple number, and it gives you time to fix things while they're still small.

steps.h: Example: three weeks of review results
steps.p: Example numbers only. Week 1 is calm. Week 2 the rate jumps after a new angle launched. Week 3 the buyer keeps launching the same angle. A pattern like this often comes before an account restriction.
steps.more: Check the maths: 2 ÷ 40 = 0.05 = 5%. 6 ÷ 40 = 0.15 = 15%. 11 ÷ 44 = 0.25 = 25%. The right move in week 2 was to stop launching that angle, read every rejection reason and fix the root cause. Meta does not publish a rejection rate that triggers a ban, so treat any rise as a warning, not a safe zone.
steps.say: Here's an example, with example numbers only. In week one, two of forty ads were rejected, five percent. Calm. In week two, after a new angle launched, six of forty, so fifteen percent. In week three the buyer kept launching that same angle, and eleven of forty four were rejected, twenty five percent. A pattern like this often comes before a restriction. The right move in week two was to stop that angle, read every reason and fix the cause. Meta doesn't publish a rate that triggers a ban, so treat any rise as a warning.

steps.h: Warning signs build before a ban
steps.p: Example pattern. Rejections climb while the buyer keeps raising spend. Restrictions rarely come from nowhere; there is usually a trail of rejections, payment problems or login alerts first. Watch both lines together.
steps.say: Look at the two lines on this chart. It's an example pattern. Ads rejected per week climb from one up to eleven, while daily spend climbs from twenty dollars to two hundred and fifty. The buyer kept raising spend while the warnings piled up. Restrictions rarely come from nowhere. There's usually a trail first: rejections, payment problems, or login alerts. So watch both lines together, not just your spend.

Pause new launches

steps.say: Here's a starting rule you can adapt. Follow the flow on screen. If more than one in ten ads is rejected in a week, or three rejections land on the same angle, pause new launches in that account. Then read every reason. Fix the root cause. And relaunch one fixed ad first, before the rest. That single ad tells you whether the fix worked before you put everything back at risk.

steps.h: Most restrictions have a findable cause
steps.p: Platforms make mistakes, and honest accounts do get restricted. But most restrictions have a cause you can find in your ads, landers, payments or logins. The rest of this module shows you how to prevent it, read it and respond.

d.b: Find the cause before you react

steps.say: Let's close the lesson with the big idea. Platforms do make mistakes, and honest accounts do get restricted. But most restrictions have a cause you can find, in your ads, your landers, your payments or your logins. So find the cause before you react, and then prevent the next one. The rest of this module shows you how to prevent a restriction, read it and respond.

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll learn why ad accounts get restricted, the four levels a restriction can hit, and the early-warning number that tells you trouble is coming. Knowing this is how you protect the spend, the data and the income that sit behind every account.

lessons.title: The prevention checklist
objectives: By the end you can set up verification, two-factor authentication and admin roles the right way.
You can plan a gradual spend warm-up for a new account.
You can check a landing page and ad copy against a policy-safe checklist.

steps.h: Prevention is cheaper than any appeal
steps.p: An appeal can take days and may fail. Prevention takes a few hours once and a few minutes each day. Most of what protects an account is boring: a real identity, secure logins, a steady payment method, gradual spending and honest pages.

d.b: Hours of setup protect weeks of spend

steps.say: Here's the core idea. An appeal can take days, and it may fail. Prevention takes a few hours once, then a few minutes each day. And most of what protects an account is honestly a bit boring. A real identity. Secure logins. A steady payment method. Gradual spending. Honest pages. As the slide says, hours of setup protect weeks of spend, and boring habits keep accounts alive.

steps.h: Example: prevention cost versus ban cost
steps.p: Example numbers only. A buyer earns about $210 profit a day on $600 spend at 35% ROI. Prevention costs a few hours. One week offline costs far more than that, before counting wages or lost caps.
steps.more: Check the maths: $600 × 0.35 = $210 profit a day. Seven days × $210 = $1,470. The $400 fixed costs are an example of a week of one buyer's wage and tools that still need paying. These numbers are illustrative; results vary.
steps.say: Let's compare the two costs. These are example numbers only. A buyer earns about two hundred and ten dollars profit a day, on six hundred dollars spend at thirty five percent R O I, return on investment. Look at the table. Prevention costs about four hours once, and no lost profit. One week offline costs one thousand four hundred and seventy dollars of profit, plus four hundred dollars of fixed costs paid with no income, and your network cap may be reassigned. steps.p: These are the foundations. Every item links the account to a real, verifiable business and stops strangers getting in. If any of these is missing, fix it before you raise spend.
d: Business verified in your business portfolio
Real name and real details on every admin profile
Two-factor authentication on for every admin
Each person uses their own login
At least two trusted admins
Business email on your own domain
steps.say: These are your foundations. Go down the checklist. Business verified in your business portfolio. Real name and real details on every admin profile. Two-factor authentication on for every admin. Each person uses their own login. At least two trusted admins. And a business email on your own domain. Every item links the account to a real, verifiable business and keeps strangers out. If any of these is missing, fix it before you raise spend.

steps.h: Turn on two-factor and check verification
steps.p: Follow these steps in Meta's business settings. The menu names here are as we understand them at the time of writing; we are not certain they are current, so look for the same idea if your screen differs. Names change; check the current settings.

steps.title: Open business settings
steps.text: Go to your business portfolio and open its settings. Choose the portfolio you advertise from.

steps.title: Check verification status
steps.text: In the security area, check whether the business is verified. If not, start verification with your registered company details.

steps.title: Require two-factor
steps.text: Where the option exists, require two-factor authentication for everyone in the portfolio.

steps.say: Let's walk through it. Tap Next to follow each step. First, open business settings: go to your business portfolio, open its settings, and choose the portfolio you advertise from. Second, check verification status in the security area. If it's not verified, start verification with your registered company details. Third, where the option exists, require two-factor authentication for everyone in the portfolio. Fourth, on your own profile, switch on an authenticator app, and save your backup codes somewhere safe and offline. Menu names change, so if your screen differs, look for the same idea.

steps.p: Give each person the lowest access that lets them do their job. Admins can remove everyone else, so keep that role for two people you trust completely. Remove access the same day someone leaves.

rows: Someone can act if you are locked out

steps.say: Now, admin hygiene. The rule is simple: give each person the lowest access that lets them do their job. Look at the table. The founder is admin, because they own the business. A trusted partner is the backup admin, so someone can act if you're locked out. A media buyer gets ad account access only, so they can run ads but can't remove admins. And a freelancer gets temporary access to one account. Remember, admins can remove everyone else, and you remove access the same day someone leaves.

steps.p: Payment problems are one of the most common triggers. Use one steady method that belongs to your business, keep funds available, and never dispute a charge you genuinely owe.

Same billing country as your business
Enough funds before each billing threshold
Do not swap cards repeatedly
Never file a chargeback on ads you ran
Keep invoices for every charge
steps.say: Payment problems are one of the most common triggers, so let's get this right. Use a card or account in your business or your own name. Keep the same billing country as your business. Have enough funds before each billing threshold. Don't swap cards repeatedly. Never file a chargeback on ads you actually ran. And keep invoices for every charge. One steady method that belongs to you builds trust.

steps.p: Reviewers and users judge the page your ad sends them to. A clean page loads fast, matches the ad, says who you are and makes no promises you cannot keep. Run every lander through this list before launch.

Does the headline match the ad's promise? Are your business name and contact details visible? Are the privacy policy and terms linked? Is there a risk warning where the offer needs one? And no fake timers, fake reviews, or income promises. A clean page is honest and fast.

steps.h: Starting rule: before every budget raise
steps.p: Starting rule to adapt: raise daily budget by no more than about 20 to 30% at a time, and only when the last three days had no new rejections, no payment failures and no login alerts. If any is present, fix it first.

No rejections or payment issues

steps.say: Here's a starting rule for every budget raise. Follow the flow. First ask, were the last three days clean? No new rejections, no payment issues, and no new login alerts. Only then raise the daily budget, by no more than about twenty to thirty percent at a time. Then wait two to three days and repeat. If any warning is present, fix it first, before you raise anything.

steps.text: Check for unknown logins, new admins or changed emails. Change your password, confirm 2FA and remove anyone you do not recognise.

steps.text: Pause anything elsewhere that shares the likely cause. Keep unrelated compliant campaigns at their current budget. Do not raise them.

steps.title: Hour 3 to 4: fix or appeal
steps.text: Fix what clearly breaks a rule. If the decision looks wrong, submit one calm appeal with evidence.

steps.h: What never to do on ban day
steps.p: Never create new profiles, portfolios or ad accounts to keep advertising while restricted. Never move the restricted ads or landers to another account. Never use someone else's account. Meta treats these as circumvention, and it can spread the restriction to everything you own.

d.text: Opening new assets or using other people's accounts to continue after a restriction is circumvention. It often ends with every linked asset banned.

steps.p: Your affiliate manager would rather hear it from you today than notice your volume vanish. Be brief and factual: what happened, the expected impact, what you are doing and when you will update. Do not blame the platform or promise dates you cannot control.

steps.p: Runway tells you how long you can keep paying fixed costs if income slows. Work it out on ban day so decisions about wages, tools and spend come from numbers, not fear.

steps.say: Runway tells you how long you can keep paying fixed costs if income slows. Look at the equation: cash available, divided by fixed costs per day, equals days of runway. Work it out on ban day, so your decisions about wages, tools and spend come from numbers, not fear.

steps.p: Example numbers only. The team has $3,000 cash and $150 a day of fixed costs, so 20 days of runway. A $2,400 payout is due on net 30 terms. The account matters, but the business is not in danger this week.
steps.more: Check the maths: $3,000 ÷ $150 = 20 days. Net 30 means the network pays 30 days after the period ends, so that $2,400 is not cash you can use today. Ask the network whether the restriction affects any pending payouts; it usually should not if your traffic was compliant, but confirm. If runway were under 10 days, the starting rule is to cut non-essential costs the same day.

lessons.title: Building resilience inside the rules
objectives: By the end you can design a setup where one restriction does not stop your business.
You can build owned audiences and diversified traffic the honest way.
You can explain why buying, renting, farming, cloaking and evasion destroy businesses.

steps.p: If one account, one admin or one traffic source can switch off all your income, you do not have a business yet; you have a risk. Resilience means legitimate backups you actually own, spread across assets, people and channels.

d.b: One switch should never turn off everything

steps.say: Here's the test of a real business. If one account, one admin or one traffic source can switch off all your income, you don't have a business yet. You have a risk. Resilience means legitimate backups you actually own, spread across assets, people and channels. One switch should never turn off everything. Spread risk the honest way.

steps.h: Example: a week offline, two setups
steps.p: Example numbers only. Both buyers earn $250 profit a day and have $600 a week in fixed costs. Buyer A has everything on one ad account. Buyer B has the same income spread so Meta is 55% of profit. Meta is offline for a week for both.

B keeps $787.50 from other channels, minus $600 fixed costs, leaving about +$187. Same skill, very different week. Figures are illustrative; results vary.

steps.p: Before you add any backup, ask these questions in order. If any answer is no, it is not a backup; it is evasion, and it will hurt you.
d: Do I really own it?
Is it in my real name or business?
Would I show it to a reviewer?
Does it follow the platform rules?
Yes to all: it is a backup
steps.say: Here's the resilience test. Ask these questions in order before you add any backup. Do I really own it? Is it in my real name or business? Would I show it to a reviewer? Does it follow the platform rules? Only if the answer is yes to all of them is it a backup. If any answer is no, it's not a backup. It's evasion, and it will hurt you.

steps.h: Why bought or rented accounts fail
steps.p: Buying or renting ad accounts, profiles or portfolios looks like a shortcut. It breaks platform terms and usually ends badly. You do not control the identity behind it, and it links your business to whoever did.
d: Banned with links|platforms often restrict linked assets
Not your identity|you cannot verify or appeal honestly
Theft risk|the seller can take it back or empty it
Legal risk|using someone's identity can be fraud
steps.say: Buying or renting ad accounts, profiles or portfolios looks like a shortcut. It breaks platform terms and usually ends badly. Look at the cards. Banned with links, because platforms often restrict linked assets. Not your identity, so you can't verify or appeal honestly. Theft risk, because the seller can take it back or empty it. And legal risk, because using someone's identity can be fraud.

steps.p: Example numbers only, to show why shortcuts lose. A buyer rents an account for $150, spends $900 on aggressive ads, and the account is banned on day 9. The network sees cloaked traffic and claws back commissions.
steps.more: Check the maths: −$150 − $900 + $1,400 − $1,400 = −$1,050. Many network terms let them withhold or reverse commissions for traffic that breaks their rules or the platform's, and to close the affiliate account. Your own verified assets may also be restricted if they are linked. This is an illustrative example; outcomes vary, and some are worse.
steps.say: Here's the rented-account maths, with example numbers only, to show why shortcuts lose. A buyer rents an account for one hundred and fifty dollars and spends nine hundred on aggressive ads. They earn one thousand four hundred dollars in commissions, before review. The account is banned on day nine, the network sees cloaked traffic and claws back the full one thousand four hundred. The net is minus one thousand and fifty dollars, plus a ban from the network. This is illustrative, and some outcomes are worse.

steps.p: These are the shortcuts we refuse to teach. Each one tries to hide from a platform's rules. Each one puts the whole business, and sometimes your freedom, at risk.
d: Account farming|making fake profiles to age and sell; breaks terms
Cloaking|showing reviewers a different page; seen as deception
Ban evasion|new assets to continue after a restriction
Network fallout|clawbacks, closed accounts, blacklists
steps.say: These are the shortcuts we refuse to teach. Account farming, making fake profiles to age and sell, which breaks terms. Cloaking, showing reviewers a different page, which is seen as deception. Ban evasion, creating new assets to continue after a restriction. And the network fallout that follows: clawbacks, closed accounts and blacklists. Each one puts the whole business, and sometimes your freedom, at risk.

steps.p: Platforms can restrict every asset linked to evasion. Networks can withhold payouts and close accounts. Fake identities and deceptive pages can break consumer and fraud laws. We do not teach any of these, and we ask you not to use them.

exam.q: You submitted 60 ads this week and 9 were rejected, 5 on the same angle. Spend is $200 a day. What do you do?
options: Move the angle to another account
Pause new launches, read every reason, fix the angle, relaunch one fixed ad
exam.why: 9 ÷ 60 = 15%, above the 10% starting rule, with 5 on one angle. Fix the root cause; moving it elsewhere is circumvention.

exam.q: Account Quality shows your personal profile restricted, but all ad accounts look active. How serious is this?
options: Not serious, the accounts are fine
Serious: you may be unable to manage ads, and you are a single point of failure if you are the only admin
exam.why: A restricted profile can stop you managing ads. That is why a trusted backup admin matters.

exam.q: Your ad said 'double your money in a week'. It was rejected and the account restricted. Best move?
options: Remove the claim, fix the copy and lander, then request review stating what you changed
Run it in a new account
Ask the network to complain to Meta
exam.why: The claim breaks the rules, so fix it first. An honest review request can mention the correction.

exam.q: Example: 5 ad accounts at $100 a day each; one is disabled. What share of spend stops, and what do you do with the other four?
options: 20%; raise the others by 25% to recover volume
20%; keep unrelated compliant ones steady, pause any sharing the cause, no budget raises
exam.why: $100 ÷ $500 = 20%. Pause only what shares the cause and freeze raises.

exam.q: On ban day you find an unknown admin added to your portfolio yesterday. What comes first?
options: Remove the unknown admin, change passwords, confirm 2FA, report the compromise
exam.why: A stranger inside means a possible hack. Secure the business before anything else.

exam.q: Cash $1,800, fixed costs $200 a day, payout of $3,000 due on net 30. What is your runway and what follows?
exam.why: $1,800 ÷ $200 = 9 days. The net 30 payout is not usable cash today, so under 10 days means cutting non-essential costs now.

exam.q: You lack your company registration certificate for an appeal. A friend offers to edit theirs with your name. What do you do?
options: Ask an agency to make one
Refuse; explain honestly and send what genuine documents you have
exam.why: False documents can make a ban permanent and can be a crime. Honesty keeps the problem fixable.

exam.q: A seller offers an aged ad account with a high spend limit for $300. Why is this a bad deal?
options: It breaks platform terms, links your business to an identity you do not control, and risks bans and clawbacks
It is fine if the network agrees
exam.why: Renting or buying accounts is prohibited and often leads to linked bans and network clawbacks.

exam.q: Your new account spent $20 a day for 3 clean days. The new offer looks great. What is a sensible next budget?
options: $24 to $26, then reassess in 2 to 3 days

exam.q: Buyer A earns 100% of profit from one ad account; Buyer B earns 50% from Meta, 30% from a Telegram channel, 20% from a second source. Both earn $300 a day and Meta pauses for 5 days. How much profit does each lose?
exam.why: 5 × $300 = $1,500. A loses all of it; B loses 50%, $750. Diversified, legitimate channels halve the damage.
